title: Characterization of Priority-Neutral Matching Lattices
abstract: We study the structure of the set of priority-neutral matchings. These matchings, introduced by Reny (2022), generalize stable matchings by allowing for priority violations in a principled way that enables Pareto-improvements to stable matchings. Known results show that the set of priority-neutral matchings is a lattice, suggesting that these matchings may enjoy the same tractable theoretical structure as stable matchings. In this paper, we characterize priority-neutral matching lattices, and show that their structure is considerably more intricate than that of stable matching lattices. To begin, we show priority-neutral lattices are not distributive, an important property that characterizes stable lattices and is satisfied by many other lattice structures considered in matching theory and algorithm design. Then, in our main result, we show that priority-neutral lattices are in fact characterized by a more-involved property which we term being a "movement lattice," which allows for significant departures from the order theoretic properties of distributive (and hence stable) lattices. While our results show that priority-neutrality is more intricate than stability, they also establish tractable properties. Indeed, as a corollary of our main result, we obtain the first known polynomial-time algorithm for checking whether a given matching is priority-neutral.

Abstract—We study the structure of the set of
priority-neutral matchings. These matchings, introduced
by [Ren22], generalize stable matchings by allowing for
priority violations in a principled way that enables Paretoimprovements to stable matchings. Known results show
that the set of priority-neutral matchings is a lattice, suggesting that these matchings may enjoy the same tractable
theoretical structure as stable matchings.
In this paper, we characterize priority-neutral matching
lattices, and show that their structure is considerably more
intricate than that of stable matching lattices. To begin,
we show priority-neutral lattices are not distributive, an
important property that characterizes stable lattices and
is satisﬁed by many other lattice structures considered in
matching theory and algorithm design. Then, in our main
result, we show that priority-neutral lattices are in fact
characterized by a more-involved property which we term
being a “movement lattice,” which allows for signiﬁcant
departures from the order theoretic properties of distributive (and hence stable) lattices. While our results show
that priority-neutrality is more intricate than stability, they
also establish tractable properties. Indeed, as a corollary
of our main result, we obtain the ﬁrst known polynomialtime algorithm for checking whether a given matching is
priority-neutral.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Stable matchings are a foundational notion in the
theory of matching under preferences. Since their introduction in [GS62], they have been found to exhibit a both
textbook algorithmic elegance and rich theoretical structure [Knu76], [Bla84], [GI89], [KT06]. These insights
culminate in a striking characterization: when matchings
are ordered according to agents’ preferences, the set of
stable matchings forms a distributive lattice.1 Moreover,
every distributive lattice arises in this way, so this

property precisely characterizes the structure of stable

for countless results on stable matchings, including their
combinatorics (e.g., [KGW18], [PP22]), communication
(e.g., [GNOR19], [ABKS20], [GT24]), and algorithms
(e.g., [Man13], [EIV23]).
Despite these successes, there are compelling reasons
to look beyond stable matchings. For instance, in the
crucial real-world setting of student-to-school assignment [AS03], [APRS05], [APR05], [Sön23], stability
may not be a binding requirement, and is often overly
restrictive. First, regardless of the schools’ priorities,
students are typically unable to attend a school that
the centralized algorithm did not assign them to. Thus,
priority violations in matching μ—i.e., pairs (d, h) where
h d μ(d) and d h μ(h)—may create a sense of
unfairness, but may not compromise the integrity of
the matching overall. Second, stability implies forgoing
Pareto-optimality for the students. For instance, [APR09]
report that in 2006 in New York City, over 4,000 grade
8 students could be made better off without worsening
the match of any student. This leads to an important
question: is there a natural class of matchings which
permits Pareto-improvements to stable matchings, while
paying due respect to priority violations?2
Motivated by this question, the recent breakthrough
work [Ren22] proposes a generalization of stability,
termed priority-neutrality. When matching applicants to
institutions, a matching μ is priority-neutral if, for each
applicant d whose priority is violated by μ, it is not
possible for another matching ν to make d better off,
unless ν also violates the priority of some applicant who
is made worse off. Since stable matchings violate no
applicant’s priority, every stable matching is priorityneutral. But unlike stable matchings, priority-neutral
matchings also allow for violations of d’s priority when,

[Ren22] proves that priority-neutral matchings always
Pareto-improve upon stable matchings, and include a
Pareto-optimal matching. Moreover, he shows their set
has structure: like stable matchings, the set of priorityneutral matchings forms a lattice.3 Thus, known results
seem to suggest that—in addition to offering improvements in applicants’ welfare—priority-neutral matchings
may be as theoretically tractable as stable matchings.
a) Our Results.: In this paper, we show that the
structure of the priority-neutral lattice is in fact far more
involved than that of the stable lattice. Our ﬁrst result
(Section III) begins by answering an open question of
[Ren22], and showing that the priority-neutral lattice is
not distributive. Moreover, we show that in the priorityneutral lattice, the greatest lower bound of two matchings
is not their coordinatewise minimum (as it is in the
stable matching lattice, and in many other lattices of
algorithmic interest, e.g., [PQ80], [KNK93], [GS99]).4
These facts imply that priority-neutral matchings lack
much of the tractable structure of stable matchings. (For
instance, they show that the priority-neutral lattice cannot
be represented by a partial order on a set of rotations,
the classic strengthening of Birkhoff’s representation
theorem [Bir37] for the stable lattice which underpins
the results discussed above.)
Given that priority-neutral lattices thus lack the
tractable structure of stable matching lattices, we ask the
following questions: What lattices do arise as priorityneutral matching lattices? What properties to priorityneutral lattices satisfy, and how can we represent their
structure?
In our main result, we characterize priority-neutral
matching lattices. That is, we provide a representation of
the set of priority-neutral matchings, and moreover, we
delineate the exact class of lattices which can arise in this
way. This class—which we call movement lattices—is

fairly intricate, and we show via examples that priorityneutral lattices can have order-theoretic structure quite
different from that of distributive lattices. Moreover,
proving that this representation captures priority-neutral
matching lattices is involved: we build on an extensive theory of different matching lattices that generalize
stability, and use techniques from [Kes10], [TY14],
[EM20], [Ren22], [FZ22]. For some preliminary intuition, see below.
While our results imply that priority-neutral lattices
are more intricate than stable ones, they also show ways
in which priority-neutrality is tractable. For instance, our
characterization directly yields a poly-time algorithm for
checking whether a given matching is priority-neutral.
Prior to our work, it was far from clear how to efﬁciently
check whether a matching μ is priority-neutral, since
the deﬁnition of priority-neutrality requires verifying
that no alternative matching ν satisﬁes some condition
(speciﬁcally, ν cannot improve the match of an applicant
whose priority is violated in μ without violating the
priority of an applicant who is worse off in ν).
b) Intuition for Our Results.: Intuitively, the structure of the stable matching lattice is derived from the fact
that avoiding priority violations—i.e., pairs (d, h) with
h d μ(d) and d h μ(h)—enforces simple orderingbased constraints on the set of stable matchings. For
instance, in any stable matching μ which sets μ(h) = d0 ,
consider any potential priority-violating pair (d, h) with
d h d0 . Then, to preserve stability, we must guarantee
that μ matches d at least as well as h, i.e., μ(d) d h.
Thus, this potential priority violation gives a natural
ordering structure on the differences between stable
matchings: any time h is made worse-off than d, we
must in turn make d better-off than h.

Unfortunately, avoiding priority-correcting adjustments does not enforce the same simple ordering structure on the set of priority-neutral matchings (compared
to the simple structure that avoiding priority violations
enforces on the set of stable matchings). Intuitively, this
is because if μ violates d’s priority, and if a potential
priority-correcting adjustment ν violates the priority of
multiple applicants dx and dy , then this ν can witness
the fact that μ is not priority-neutral only if neither dx
or dy have been made better off than their match in
ν. Hence, the change that violates d’s priority can be
made after either dx or dy have been improved. The
resulting ordering structure can be much more intricate
than those that (by Birkhoff’s theorem) underpin stable
and distributive lattices (which could only require, for
example, that both dx and dy must have been improved).
In our ﬁrst result (in Section III), we construct an
instance implementing the above idea for priority-neutral
lattices, showing that they are not distributive. After
this, we directly pursue a generalization of the above
discussion, and attempt to capture the order-theoretic
constraints induced by priority-correcting adjustments
in terms of a “multiple predecessor” generalization of
results for stable lattices. While this approach allows us

to prove some structural results on the set of priority neutral matchings, it does not give a tight characterization.
Hence, in our main result, we take a more “low level”
approach, and encode the data of a priority-correcting
adjustment into a direct representation. In the end, this
low-level approach gives a tight characterization.
c) Related Work.: Our paper builds most directly
on two strands of literature. First, we build on a vast
literature on the structure of stable matchings following from the seminal [GS62]. For structural properties
speciﬁcally, [GI89] is the classical reference; see also
[EIV23, Section 1.4] or [CT19]. Key individual works
include [Knu74], [Bla84], [IL86], which establish that
stable matching lattices are exactly characterized by distributive lattices. Other works establishing fundamental
properties of stable matching mechanisms include, for
example, [GS85a], [MW71], [Rot82], [Rot84], [DF81],
[GS85b].
Second, we build on papers studying Paretoimprovements of stable matchings. [Kes10] introduces
a mechanism known as EADAM, which has become a
centerpoint of this literature. [TY14] provides a simpler
algorithm for computing EADAM. [Ren22] introduces
priority-neutral matchings, proves they form a lattice,
and proves that the applicant-optimal matching in this
lattice equals the outcome of EADAM.
Other than priority-neutral matchings, likely the
most signiﬁcant prior theoretical framework for Paretoimproving the set of stable matchings is the set of
legal matchings [EM20], which we denote by L; see
Footnote 3 for a deﬁnition. [EM20] proves that L forms
a lattice, and the applicant-optimal matching in L equals
the outcome of EADAM. [Ren22] proves that every
priority-neutral matching is legal (and that there can be
legal, but not priority-neutral, matchings). Thus, these
two matching lattices are closely related. Throughout
this paper, we exploit the connection between priorityneutrality and legality, along with additional structural
results on legality proven by [FZ22]. However, we note
that [EM20] show that L forms a distributive lattice
which is closed under coordinatewise minimum and
maximum operations. In contrast, we prove the priorityneutral lattice is not distributive, and hence is quite
different in structure from the legal or stable lattice.
Many variations on stable matching have been proposed. [EM20] follows the general idea of “stable sets”
as in [NM44]; other papers taking similar or related approaches include [Ehl07], [MVV11], [AMV22], [DE23],
among others. [TDK20] deﬁne essentially stable matchings, which allow for Pareto-optimal matchings, but does
not form a lattice (or characterize a unique Paretooptimal matchings). [ACP+ 20], [KS20], [TZ21] compare mechanisms by the sets of priorities they violate.
[CM23] studies a generalization of strategyproofness

satisﬁed by EADAM. [RTZ23] gives a novel characterization of EADAM, as do many of the previouslymentioned papers.
In certain more-general matching problems, stable
matchings are known to form a non-distributive lattice.
Speciﬁcally, this is the case in many-to-many [Bla88]
and many-to-one [EO04] matching settings with substitutes preferences; in fact, the recent paper [EF25] shows
that all ﬁnite lattices can arise as the stable lattice in
this model. These facts crucially use the generality of
multi-partner matching with substitutes in preferences;
indeed, when preferences are responsive (i.e., institutions
preferences are consistent with a preference list over
applicants) [Rot86], or when they satisfy the commonlyassumed law of aggregate demand [Fle03], [HM05],
stable matchings form a distributive lattice [Alk02],
[Li14]. We believe it is very interesting that priorityneutral lattices have a non-distributive and fundamentally
new structure, despite being deﬁned in the completely
standard one-to-one matching model involving no new
primitives.
Following [Knu74], [GI89], lattice properties of stable matchings have been instrumental in many results.
[KGW18], [PP22] make use the rotation poset to make
breakthrough progress on the combinatorial problem of
determining the maximum possible number of distinct
stable matchings as a function of n, the number of
applicants and institutions. [GT24] designs a blackboard
veriﬁcation (in the sense of NP) communication protocol for the applicant-optimal stable mechanism. Much
algorithmic work on different variants of such matching
problems also exploits rotation poset representations
and distributive lattice properties, see e.g. [Man13],
[EIV23]. Additionally, [IL86], [SS15] use related arguments to show that counting stable matchings, and
other combinatorial matching problems, are #P-hard,
and [Sub94], [CFL14] show that stable matchings are
connected to a circuit model with “comparator” gates,
and to certain novel complexity classes between NL and
P. Further from our work, [Pit89], [IM05], [AKL17],
[GMM21], [KMQ21], [Mau21], [CT22] study stable
matchings under certain random preference distributions. Additionally, different (non-stable) matchings have
been deﬁned using ordinal preferences. One example is
popular matchings following [AIKM07]; the structural
properties of stable matchings have found applications
for this set of matchings as well [Kav24]. Another line
of work investigates the extent to which natural decentralized matching dynamics converge to stable matchings
[RV90], [AGM+ 08], [Rud24].5

for future work.

II. P RELIMINARIES
A. The Stable Matching Lattice
We begin by recalling the deﬁnition of stable matchings and their essential properties.
a) Stabile Matchings and Priority Violations.:
We study one-to-one matchings between applicants A
and institutions I (outside of some exposition in the
introduction, where we referred to students and schools,
respectively). We typically use notations like μ, ν, ξ for
matchings and (to avoid the common variables a and
i) we write d ∈ A, h ∈ I (mnemonic: doctors and
hospitals). For d ∈ A, we write μ(d) ∈ I ∪ {∅} for
d’s match, where μ(d) = ∅ denotes going unmatched
(and likewise with μ(h) for h ∈ I).
Agents on each side have a strict ordinal preference
list over the other side, i.e., rankings d over I for each
d ∈ A, and likewise h over A for h ∈ I. We refer
to these rankings of applicants as their preferences, but
by convention, we refer to the rankings of institutions
as priorities (reﬂecting the fact that, as in many school
choice mechanisms, we think of the priorities as ﬁxed
and/or determined by policies, instead of reﬂecting the
institution’s preferences). Following [Ren22], we assume
for simplicity that each institution ranks all applicants;
we allow applicants’ lists to be partial (i.e., they can
rank some “outside option” ∅, which represents going
unmatched, above some institutions).
Deﬁnition II.1 (Stable matchings and priority violations). A matching μ is unstable if there exists a d ∈ A
and h ∈ I such that h d μ(d) and d h μ(h). In this
case, we say that d’s priority is violated (at h). If there
are no such d and h, we say that μ is stable. Let Stab
denote the set of all stable matchings.
For a matching μ, denote the set of applicants whose
priority is violated in μ by
vio(μ) = {d ∈ A | ∃h ∈ I : d h μ(h) and h d μ(d)}.

b) (Stable) Lattices.: This paper studies lattice
structures on sets of matchings. A (ﬁnite) lattice Q is a
partial order ≤ over a (ﬁnite) set Q such that every pair
of elements in Q have a meet and a join. The meet (also
called the greatest lower bound) of x, y ∈ Q, denoted
x ∧Q y, is the element z ∈ Q such that z ≤ x and z ≤ y,
and moreover for each w ∈ Q such that w ≤ x and
w ≤ y, we have w ≤ z. Likewise, the join (also called
the least upper bound) of x, y ∈ Q, denoted x ∨Q y,
is the element z ∈ Q such that z ≥ x and z ≥ y, and
for each w ∈ Q such that w ≥ x and w ≥ y, we have
w ≥ z. A lattice Q is distributive if, for each x, y, z ∈ Q,
we have μ ∧Q (ν ∨Q ξ) = (μ ∧Q ν) ∨Q (μ ∧Q ξ).
We say that matching μ (weakly) dominates matching
ν, denoted μ ≥ ν, if for each applicant d we have
μ(d) d ν(d). We write μ > ν if μ ≥ ν and μ = ν.
Throughout this entire paper, the matchings are ordered
by dominance.
For two matchings μ, ν, let the coordinatewise maximum (resp., minimum) of μ and ν be the function
ξ from applicants to institutions given by ξ(d) =
maxd {μ(d), ν(d)} (resp., ξ(d) = mind {μ(d), ν(d)}).
In some (but not all) of the latices we consider, joins/meets are given by coordinatewise maxima/minima.
It is classically known that stable matchings form a
distributive lattice with joins/meets given by coordinatewise maxima/minima, and that all distributive lattices
arise as the set of stable matchings [Knu76], [Bla84].
For exposition, see [GI89], [EIV23].
Theorem II.2 (Distributive Lattices Characterize Stable Matchings). The set of stable matchings is always
nonempty, and forms a lattice under the dominance
ordering. In this lattice, the join (resp., meet) of any
two stable matchings is their coordinatewise maximum
(resp., minimum). Moreover, a lattice Q is isomorphic to
a lattice of stable matchings for some set of preferences
and priorities if and only if Q is distributive.

compact and useful representation in terms of a concept
called “rotations” [GI89], [EIV23]. For ease of exposition, we begin by using rotations only as notation for

A rotation is an ordered list of agents α = [(h1 , d1 ),

k. Hence, the action of a rotation can be visualized as

B. The Priority-Neutral Matching Lattice
As discussed in the introduction, there are important
reasons to look beyond the set of stable matchings. We
ﬁrst discuss a speciﬁc matching mechanism EADAM
which improves applicants’ matches beyond their stable
ones, and will be important for our analysis. Then we
recall the main notion we are interested in: priorityneutrality.

efﬁciency-adjusted DA mechanism (EADAM). One approach to deﬁning EADAM, pioneered by [TY14], is as

A matching μ is priority-neutral if there does not exist
any priority-correcting adjustment of μ. We denote the
set of priority-neutral matchings by PN.

Priority-correcting adjustments capture failures of
priority-neutrality; indeed, [Ren22] argues they “correct”
some applicant d’s priority violation (without unduly
harming others). In other words, priority-neutral matchings allow for some applicants’ priority to be violated,
but only when such applicants cannot be improved
without harming others and also violating their priority.
Observe that, since stable matchings violate no applicant’s priority, every stable matching is priority-neutral.
Thus, PN generalizes the set of stable matchings, and
[Ren22] proves that PN also forms a lattice. Moreover,
[Ren22] proves that the set PN is closed under the
coordinatewise maximum operation, and identiﬁes IPDA
and EADAM as the applicant-pessimal and applicantoptimal elements of PN, respectively. Formally:
Theorem II.5 ( [Ren22]). For any proﬁle of priorities
and preferences, PN is a lattice under ≤, and this
lattice contains every stable matching. Additionally, the
applicant-pessimal element of PN is IPDA, and the
applicant-optimal element of PN is EADAM. Finally, for
any two matchings μ, ν in PN, the least upper bound of
μ and ν in PN equals their coordinatewise maximum.
Note, however, that [Ren22] leaves as an open question whether the greatest lower bound of two matchings
in PN is their coordinatewise minimum. Our ﬁrst result
below resolves this question.

and that greatest lower bounds in PN are not given by
coordinatewise minimums.

We now formally show that αβ ∈ PN. Suppose for
contradiction that there exists a priority-correcting adjustment ν of αβ. Since the only applicant in αβ whose
priority is violated in dZ , we know that ν must improve
the match of dZ , so ν(dZ ) = hC or ν(dZ ) = hE . We
consider these two cases. In the ﬁrst case, if ν(dZ ) = hC ,
then ν(dD ) must be hD (since dD must receive a worse
match in ν than in αβ, where αβ(dD ) = hC , and dD
has highest-priority at hD , which is dD ’s top choice after
hC ). But, then ν(dC ) must be hC (since similarly dC
must receive a worse match in ν than in αβ, and dC
has top priority at hC ), however, this contradicts the
assumption that dZ is matched to hC in matching ν.
In the second case, suppose ν(dZ ) = hE . Since dE has
higher priority than dZ at hE , we know dE must be
matched in ν to an institution she prefers to hE ; so we
either have ν(dE ) = hA or ν(dE ) = hF . If ν(dE ) = hA ,
then dB must receive a worse match in ν than in αβ;
since dB has higher priority at hA than dE , this would
mean ν cannot be a priority-correcting adjustment, so we
cannot have ν(hE ) = hA . If ν(dE ) = hF , then ν(dF )
must be different from αβ(dF ) = hF ; since dF has
higher priority at hE than dZ and dF ’s preference list
is hE  hF , this makes it impossible that ν(dZ ) = hE ,
and we cannot have ν(dE ) = hF . Thus, this shows that
there exists no priority-correcting adjustment ν of αβ,
so αβ ∈ PN.
We now formally show that βγ ∈ PN. Again, assume
for contradiction there is a priority-correcting adjustment
ν of βγ. Since dZ is the only applicant whose priority
is violated in βγ, we must have ν(dZ ) = hC or
